title: The Spice Islands — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 1
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 1 · Student Reader pp. 2–9
bigQuestion: According to the author, how did the search for the Spice Islands change history?

missions.name: The Spice Islands
missions.blurb: One quiz for the whole chapter, with questions from each of its four headed sections and the Big Question at the end. Mostly what happened; four questions on the words the trade story is built from. The card says which page answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

items.hi: but also as a way to preserve it

vs.q: In medieval Europe, why did people need spices besides for flavor?
opts: To keep food from going rotten before it was eaten
To make the dyes that colored their clothes
To keep away the diseases spreading in the towns
To feed the animals kept through the winter
vs.why: To preserve it. Medieval Europe had no refrigeration, so spices did the job a fridge does now — which is why they were worth a journey halfway round the world.

vs.q: What could Europeans of this time not do, which made spices so valuable?
opts: Keep food cold in any way
Carry water to their towns
Grow any crops in winter
Cook meat over a fire
vs.why: No refrigerators, no cold storage of any kind. Spices extended the time meat and other foods could be kept and still safely eaten.

vs.q: The chapter says spices were very expensive. Why?
opts: They grew in faraway Asia, and the trip was dangerous
The plants had almost died out and were rare
European rulers taxed every spice that was sold
Few cooks in Europe knew how to use them
vs.why: Distance and danger, not scarcity of the plants. Everything that long journey cost ended up in the price.

vs.q: Which spices does the chapter name as grown in faraway Asia?
opts: Pepper, cinnamon, ginger, and cloves
Vanilla, saffron, and bay leaves
Garlic, onion, and mustard seed
Mint, parsley, sage, and thyme
vs.why: Those four, plus other seasonings. Every one of them had to come the whole way from Asia, which is the reason the rest of the chapter happens.

vs.q: The Spice Islands are part of which archipelago?
opts: The Malay Archipelago
The Caribbean Archipelago
The Aegean Archipelago
The Canary Archipelago
vs.why: The Malay Archipelago, in present-day Indonesia — a chain of more than thirteen thousand islands on the far side of Asia from Europe.

vs.q: The Malay Archipelago stretches between which two places?
opts: The Malay Peninsula and Australia
Arabia and the coast of Egypt
India and the coast of Africa
Southern China and Japan
vs.why: From the Malay Peninsula in Southeast Asia all the way down to Australia. The Spice Islands are a handful of islands inside that long chain.

hi: Heat, heavy rainfall, and rich soil

vs.q: Why do the Spice Islands grow such exceptional spice crops?
opts: Heat, heavy rainfall, and rich soil
Cool nights and a long dry season
Gentle rain spread evenly all year
Sandy soil that drains after storms
vs.why: Three things together, and the chapter names all three. It is why these islands in particular were worth crossing the world for.

vs.q: One side of these mountains gets up to 320 inches of rain a year. What does the chapter call the dry side?
opts: The rain shadow side
The forest side
The coastal side
The volcano side
vs.why: The rain shadow side, where it can be under twenty inches a year. The mountain catches the weather, and the far side sits in its shadow.

hi: Nor were their ships and navigational skills suited
keep the location of the Spice Islands a secret

vs.q: Why didn't Europeans just sail over to the Spice Islands and buy spices?
opts: Their ships and skills were not up to the voyage
The Arabs guarded the sea route with warships
Their rulers had forbidden such long voyages
They had no way to pay for such a voyage
vs.why: Their ships and navigational skills could not manage voyages that long, they did not yet know the Atlantic reached the southern tip of Africa, and nobody in Europe knew where the islands were.

vs.q: What did the Arabs manage to keep secret from about 1100 until 1400?
opts: Where the Spice Islands were
How spices were dried and packed
Which spices Europe wanted most
When their ships left for Asia
vs.why: The location. Three hundred years of it, helped along by stories of sea monsters and flesh-eating birds guarding the islands.

hi: preserve their monopoly of the spice trade

vs.q: What does the chapter mean by a trader?
opts: A person who buys and sells goods
A person who sails a ship for a living
A person who guards a storehouse
A person who makes goods by hand
vs.why: Somebody who buys and sells. Keep it next to merchant, which the chapter uses for the other end of the same route.

vs.q: What is a monopoly?
opts: Complete control of the supply of a good
A market where goods are bought and sold
A tax on goods brought into a country
An agreement between two trading countries
vs.why: Complete control of the supply. The second answer is closer to a trading center, a different word from this same chapter, and worth keeping apart.

hi: the spice trade was controlled by Arab traders
made up stories about how dangerous it was

vs.q: In the Middle Ages, the spice trade was controlled by traders from which background?
opts: Arab traders
Chinese traders
Spanish traders
Mongol traders
vs.why: Arab traders. They controlled the market not only for nutmeg and cloves from the Spice Islands, but for ginger from China and cinnamon from India as well.

vs.q: How did the monster stories help the Arab traders keep their monopoly?
opts: If nobody dared go, nobody else could supply them
They frightened the Venetians into paying more
They explained to buyers why spices cost so much
They stopped their own sailors from leaving
vs.why: A monopoly lasts only while nobody else can reach the supply. Flesh-eating birds and sea monsters were cheaper than guarding the route, and they worked for three hundred years.

vs.q: The chapter calls the Venetians merchants. What is a merchant?
opts: A person who buys and sells goods to earn money
A person who records everything a ship carries
A person who lends money to shipowners
A person who carries goods for a fee
vs.why: Almost the same as a trader, and that is the point: the chapter gives one word to each end of the route, Arab traders at one end and Venetian merchants at the other.

vs.q: What is a trading center?
opts: A place where people buy and sell goods
A ship built to carry goods a long way
A tax office at a country's border
A storehouse where spices are kept dry
vs.why: A place where buying and selling happen. The Arab traders sailed east to several of them, loaded up, and sailed west again.

vs.q: In Egypt, who did the Arab traders sell the spices to?
opts: Merchants from Venice and other parts of Italy
Merchants who had sailed down from England
Merchants travelling overland from China
Merchants sent out by the king of Spain
vs.why: Venetian merchants, in Egypt. The spices changed hands there, and the Arab traders took huge profits from the exchange before the Venetians took theirs.

vs.q: Arab traders sailed east to trading centers in which places?
opts: India, Ceylon, and the Spice Islands
Arabia, Persia, and the Red Sea
Egypt, Venice, and Genoa
China, Japan, and Korea
vs.why: Those three. They loaded their ships at the eastern end of the route, then sailed west again towards Egypt.

hi: set whatever prices and taxes they pleased
negotiated with Arab traders to distribute spices

vs.q: Once the Venetian merchants had the spices, what could they do?
opts: Set whatever prices and taxes they pleased
Sell them only inside the city of Venice
Sell them only to other merchants
Send back any they could not sell
vs.why: Anyone in Europe who wanted spices had to deal with Venice, so Venice named the price. It made the city very wealthy and, the chapter adds, very unpopular.

vs.q: What did the Venetians negotiate with the Arab traders for?
opts: The right to distribute spices through Europe
A lower price than any other buyer paid
Safe passage for their ships to Asia
A share of the Arab traders' profits
vs.why: To negotiate is to talk terms. What the Venetians talked their way into was the right to hand the spices on through Europe, which is what let them charge whatever they pleased.

hi: in the service of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan

vs.q: Who was Marco Polo?
opts: A young Venetian who travelled east with his father and uncle
An Arab trader who first found the way to the Spice Islands
A Mongol general who came west to rule Venice
A Pisan writer who sailed to China and back
vs.why: A boy from Venice. His father Niccolo and his uncle Maffeo were traders and travelers, and in 1271 they took him east with them.

vs.q: What did Marco Polo end up doing in Asia?
opts: He spent years in the service of Kublai Khan
He mapped the whole of the Malay Archipelago
He bought spices directly from the islands
He set up a trading center on the coast
vs.why: He served the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan and travelled all over Asia by land and by sea. The whole journey took the three of them twenty-four years.

hi: The Mongols made the roads safe for travelers

vs.q: Why were travelers suddenly able to cross Asia in Marco Polo's time?
opts: The Mongols had made the roads safe
The Arabs had opened the sea route
The Khan had built a road to Europe
Venice paid for guards on the way
vs.why: The Mongols controlled much of Asia and part of Europe, and they made the roads safe. That is what let the old overland routes open again and sent adventurers east after their fortunes.

vs.q: What did adventurers travel into Mongol-controlled Asia to trade for?
opts: Silk, gems, porcelain, and tea
Gold, salt, ivory, and cloth
Spices, timber, and glass
Wool, wine, and silver
vs.why: Silk, gems, porcelain and tea. Others went looking for the world's most exotic spices, which is how this section joins up with the rest of the chapter.

items.hi: sparked the Age of European Exploration

vs.q: According to the author, how did the search for the Spice Islands change history?
opts: It set off the Age of Exploration and the settling of the Americas
It made Venice the richest and most powerful city in all Europe
It ended the Middle Ages across the whole of Europe
It led to a long war between Europe and the Arabs
vs.why: This is the chapter's Big Question. Wanting the same spices for less money is what sent Europeans out across the oceans, and the author traces the settling of the Americas back to it.

vs.q: What does the author say Europe's wish for cheaper spices sparked?
opts: The Age of Exploration, and the settling of the Americas
The first ships that were able to cross an entire ocean
The end of the spice trade between Venice and the Arabs
A new overland road running from Europe into China
vs.why: The Big Question again, asked the other way round. The author goes so far as to say the United States exists today because medieval Europeans liked spicy food.

why.title: The Spice of Life — why spices mattered
vocab: relating to the Middle Ages in Europe
a plant used to add flavor to food
text: Supermarkets today stock all sorts of spices that can be used to season or add flavor to different foods. In medieval Europe, however, people relied on spices not only to flavor their food, but also as a way to preserve it.
Without refrigerators or other cold storage, medieval Europeans used spices to extend the time period during which meats and other foods could be stored and then safely eaten before turning rotten.

cost.title: The Spice of Life — what it all set off
text: In the Middle Ages, spices were hard to get. Pepper, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and other seasonings were grown in faraway Asia.
Getting the spices to Europe took a lot of time and effort. Distances were great, and travel back and forth was dangerous. As a result, spices were very expensive.
Europe's desire for cheaper spices sparked the Age of European Exploration and its settlement of the Americas.

islands.title: The Spice Islands — where they are
text: Different spices come from different places. Many of the most desirable spices come from the islands of present-day Indonesia.

Indonesia is an archipelago , or chain of islands. It stretches from Southeast Asia's Malay Peninsula to the continent of Australia. This group, known as the Malay Archipelago, contains more than thirteen thousand islands.

fire.title: The Spice Islands — why the crops are so good
vocab: an area that gets less rain because it is on the protected side of a mountain
text: Daytime temperatures are between 70 and 90 F year-round. Rainfall can be as much as 320 inches a year on the forested mountain slopes. On the rain shadow sides, it can be less than twenty inches a year.
Heat, heavy rainfall, and rich soil result in exceptional spice crops.

secret.title: The Quest for Spices — a secret worth guarding
vocab: a person who buys and sells goods
a situation in which one person, country, or company has complete control of the supply of a good or service
related to controlling the movement of a ship
a place where people buy and sell goods
text: You might wonder why the Europeans didn't just sail over to the Spice Islands and buy their spices. It wasn't that simple. They did not yet know that the Atlantic Ocean went as far as the southern tip of Africa. Nor were their ships and navigational skills suited to such long voyages.

During the Middle Ages, the spice trade was controlled by Arab traders . They controlled the market not only for nutmeg and cloves from the Spice Islands, but also for ginger from China and cinnamon from India. For hundreds of years, from around 1100 until 1400, the Arabs managed to keep the location of the Spice Islands a secret. They even made up stories about how dangerous it was to sail to these islands.

If you had been alive then you might have heard tales told by Arab traders of the fantastic monsters and hideous flesh-eating birds that guarded the Spice Islands. Stories like these were designed to help the Arab traders preserve their monopoly of the spice trade.

route.title: The Quest for Spices — how the trade worked
vocab: a person who buys and sells goods to earn money
text: How did the spice trade work? Arab traders sailed east to trading centers in India, Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), and the Spice Islands. After loading up their ships, they sailed west again.

A typical trip took them around the Arabian Peninsula, into the Red Sea, and north to Egypt. There they sold the spices to merchants from Venice and other parts of Italy. The Arab traders made huge profits from this exchange.

venice.title: The Quest for Spices — why Venice grew rich
vocab: to discuss the terms of an agreement
text: The Venetians did well, too. They negotiated with Arab traders to distribute spices throughout Europe. Europeans wanting to purchase spices had to deal with Venice.
Once they had acquired the spices, the Venetian merchants could set whatever prices and taxes they pleased. This arrangement made Venice a very wealthy city. It also made the Venetians unpopular.

polo2.title: The Travels of Marco Polo — who he was
vocab: a group of people who serve as representatives of their government in another country
text: Maffeo and Niccolo Polo were brothers who lived in Venice in the second half of the thirteenth century. The Polos were great traders and travelers.

When the Polo brothers started their second journey east in 1271, they decided to take Niccolo's young son, Marco, with them. The expedition ended up taking them twenty-four years to complete. The three spent time in the service of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan and traveled throughout Asia by land and by sea.

polo.title: The Travels of Marco Polo — the road east opens
vocab: a native of the Asian nation of Mongolia
text: When the overland trade routes that had existed in Roman times opened up again, they set out to find the legendary markets of the East. At the time, the Mongols controlled much of Asia and part of Europe.

The Mongols made the roads safe for travelers, and many adventurers were anxious to seek their fortunes. Some went to trade for silk, gems, porcelain , and tea. Others hoped to find sources of the world's most exotic spices.
